description: I'm Claire, the creator and narrator of Left Behind. I bring NASA's forgotten explorers back to life through storytelling, design, and interactive learning.
summary:
Echoes by Claire: Left Behind is a bilingual, story-driven web experience I created to give NASA’s forgotten explorers a voice. I chose the “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge to introduce learners aged 10–14 to equipment left on the Moon, Mars, and beyond, and the science these machines made possible.

Players hold to wake a machine, listen to first-person clues I recorded in my own voice, and discover its identity. Hands-on challenges connect each story to science: timing a returning laser pulse, making energy choices during a Martian dust storm, or exploring camera-based flight navigation.

I used NASA mission records and imagery to ground the experience in real exploration history. Seven main stops guide the journey, while nine optional stops invite further discovery. Players collect mission cards, receive a personalized certificate, and write a postcard to an explorer, with an option to add a preset thank you message to a shared starry sky.

Through Left Behind, I hope to help young learners see these machines as traces of human effort, each with a story that can inspire our future.
details:
Why I created Left Behind

I see the machines left across space as traces of human effort. Each carries a story of curiosity, engineering, discovery, and sometimes an unexpected ending.

For the “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge, I created Left Behind Echoes by Claire. My central idea was simple: what if the explorers we left behind could speak?

I recorded the English narration myself, giving the machines a first-person voice. These stories are creative interpretations grounded in NASA mission history, rather than authentic spacecraft transmissions. I want children to understand the explorers’ experiences and the science they made possible.

How the experience works

Left Behind is a bilingual web experience in English and Traditional Chinese, designed primarily for ages 10–14. Seven main stops guide players across the Moon, Mars, and deep space, while nine optional stops invite further discovery.

Players hold to wake a machine, listen to short clues, and discover its identity and story. Questions, estimates, and hands-on activities turn listening into participation. Each stop leads to a collectible mission card with a key number, a scientific takeaway, and supporting sources.

Different stories, different ways to explore

  • Apollo 11 laser reflector: Aim a beam, time its return, and calculate a distance to explore lunar laser ranging.
  • Opportunity: Make energy choices as a dust storm reduces sunlight, connecting the rover’s final months to the limits of solar-powered exploration.
  • Ingenuity: Hold to climb and release to descend while ground texture changes, introducing why camera-based navigation needs visible surface features.
  • Pioneer 10: Choose symbols for a message from Earth, reflecting on the spacecraft’s plaque and communication beyond our planet.

Other activities include estimating lunar-rover travel distance and detecting dips in starlight in a simplified Kepler transit game.

NASA resources and scientific accuracy

I used NASA NSSDCA mission records, NASA Science and JPL resources, and NASA imagery to inform mission dates, hardware purposes, scientific discoveries, and mission outcomes.

The games are educational simplifications. Opportunity’s power snapshots refer to reported historical measurements, while task energy costs are game values. Laser results depend on player timing, and the flight controls are not an engineering-accurate simulator.

NASA photographs, official artist concepts, NASA simulations, and AI illustrations are identified separately. Sources and credits are available within the experience and in the project README.

From discovery to connection

I connect three activities: hearing a machine’s story, exploring its science, and responding to it. My own narration gives the machines a personal presence, while the interactions connect their experiences to scientific ideas.

Players can personalize and save an explorer certificate and a postcard. If they choose, a preset thank-you message can become a clickable star in a shared sky. Custom postcard text and names remain private.

The postcard closes the story: players have listened, learned, and left a message in return. It is my way of turning “left behind” into “not forgotten.”

Design considerations

I considered age, reading load, language, pacing, scientific accuracy, and emotional connection. Short text accompanies narration, with controls to pause or continue stories. Players can review clues and open more detailed records when they want to learn more.

A seven-stop main route provides structure, optional stops support curiosity, and responsive layouts support desktop and mobile browsers.

Tools and development

I built the project using TypeScript, React, Vite, HTML, and CSS, with browser audio and canvas-based interactions. Cloudflare Pages hosts the website; Pages Functions and a D1 database support the shared postcard sky.

I recorded the English narration, and FFmpeg was used to prepare audio. Background music was sourced from Pixabay, with credits and licence links in the README. I used AI assistants to support coding and editing, and an AI image tool for selected illustrations that are labelled in the experience.

Intended impact and next steps

I hope young learners leave able to connect a machine’s purpose, the challenges it faced, and a scientific discovery it helped make possible. Mission cards, optional reflection questions, and personalized keepsakes support recall and continued curiosity. My next step is to observe young learners using the experience and assess whether they can explain a mission’s purpose and one scientific idea afterward.

Through Left Behind, I hope to help children see these machines as traces of human effort, each with a story that can inspire our future.
